The integration of multimedia elements in presentation slides has become a common practice in educational settings. However, the various formats of multimodal slides pose a significant challenge to automatic slide analysis. Existing research on presentation slide recognition has primarily focused on individual modes of input, such as text or images, with little attention paid to multimodal analysis. To address this gap, we have created a unique dataset consisting of lectures that feature multiple types of multimedia elements. This paper introduces the MM-LP dataset, a comprehensive resource that includes 1,500 diverse lectures, to facilitate research on automatic slide analysis. We have also developed a novel dataset annotation framework that captures the temporal relationships between distinct modalities of slides. An in-depth analysis of the dataset is provided, highlighting the benefits of using multimodal recognition in the context of educational lectures. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of multimodal recognition in the identification of key presentation elements, including headings, subheadings, and images. We hope that the MM-LP dataset will serve as a valuable resource for the research community, enabling the development of more effective automatic slide analysis tools. We establish a lower bound on the regret in a worst-case scenario, showing that
a policy must achieve a square root rate of convergence. This result is both
information-theoretic and computationally motivated, and aligns with existing
convergence rate bounds. We then develop a policy that achieves the same rate
of convergence. This policy is derived from a two-stage process: we first
approximate the value function using a least-squares estimator, and then use Q-
learning to determine the optimal action. We show that both stages of this policy
are nearly optimal, and that it achieves the same regret rate as the optimal
lower bound. Our findings are significant because they establish a policy that
both efficiently learns in a worst-case setting and is nearly optimal in terms of
quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical
simulations, and show that it outperforms existing policies in a wide range of
scenarios. Our work is the first to achieve a worst-case regret rate of square
root in offline reinforcement learning. This research is further extended to
handle non-episodic and non-tabular settings, and we provide empirical evidence
that our approach is effective in these scenarios as well. We make our code and
data available for others to use and build upon. Our research is the first to

Locating graphical objects within document images poses significant difficulties due to the varied nature of these images. They often incorporate intricate combinations of text, images, and graphic elements, making object detection a complex task. To address this challenge, our research presents a novel, deep learning-based approach that leverages a convolutional neural network to identify graphical objects. To enhance model accuracy, our method incorporates a graph-based algorithm that facilitates efficient region proposal generation. Additionally, our system integrates a unique, trainable loss function that promotes precise object localization. Evaluating our method on a diverse range of public image datasets, we achieve exceptional performance, with state-of-the-art results on the ICDAR2013 dataset and competitive outcomes on the COCO-Text and DII2017 datasets. Notably, our method surpasses the state-of-the-art approach on the DII2017 dataset by 2.8% in terms of mAP. Furthermore, our method's ability to accurately detect small objects and handle complex document images is demonstrated through experiments on the RIT2019C dataset. The source code for our method is available on GitHub. https://github.com/keivanB/GraphObjectDetection. We present a new online algorithm called DART (aDaptive Accept RejecT), designed to tackle the top-K subset identification issue, where the goal is to select the K suboptimal solutions from a large set of candidate solutions. DART is an adaptive rejection sampling approach that leverages a weighted sampling strategy to efficiently find the suboptimal solutions. It is the first algorithm of its kind to achieve a sublinear regret bound of O(K * sqrt(T)) while being adaptive, and it achieves this bound with a high probability. DART is also the first non-adaptive algorithm to achieve a regret bound of O(K * sqrt(T)) while being simple and scalable. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DART through experiments on the top-K subset selection in linear regression and support vector machine problems. Additionally, DART is shown to outperform state-of-the-art baselines in the top-K clustering issue. The implementation of DART is available at https://github.com/romilgupta/DART. To the best of our knowledge, DART is the first non-adaptive top-K clustering algorithm to achieve a sublinear regret bound. The Semantic Web has successfully implemented SPARQL, a standard query language, for retrieving data from various sources. However, scene graphs used in computer vision present a unique challenge due to their ability to represent complex relationships among visual entities. To address this, we propose VGStore, a multimodal extension of SPAR SparQL that enables scene graph query capabilities. By utilizing a Visual Graph Logic framework, VGStore allows for the specification of visual queries over scene graphs, which are then evaluated through a novel evaluation method. Through thorough experimentation, VGStore has demonstrated its effectiveness in accurately answering visual queries over scene graphs, even under noisy data conditions. The results of our experiments also shed light on the potential applications of VGStore, such as evaluating vision models and retrieving relevant visual information from multimodal knowledge graphs. The source code and pre-trained models for VGStore are available for public access. The link to our source code is provided at https://github.com/leeyk3/VGStore. A comprehensive analysis of the competition between alpha and beta+ weak decay processes in superheavy nuclei has been conducted. The study utilized a microscopic framework, accounting for both the alpha-emission and beta+ weak decay within a two-quasi-particle model. The research focused on nuclei ranging from Th206 to the heaviest nuclei with 112 atoms, exploring the competition between alpha decay, beta+ weak decay, and associated beta-weak decay processes. The findings reveal that alpha decay generally outlasts beta+ weak decay, yet beta+ decay can prevail over alpha decay in nuclei with 264 or more atoms. The study also discovered that the beta+ weak decay is typically the slowest decay process, followed by beta-weak decay being significantly slower. spatial relationships between a child's hands and the game's interactive elements.

child's task execution status, which is defined as correct or incorrect attempts.

cards and containers. The research findings suggest that GNN-based models can be

However, the optimal filter size varies depending on the specific application and task at hand. Our research introduces a novel approach to automatically determine the most valuable filters in a CNN model by leveraging the Self-Similarity Matrix. This matrix is constructed from the output features of the network and serves as a visual representation of the network architecture. This paper delves into advanced compiler optimizations for quantum computing, focusing on techniques such as instruction reordering, reducing quantum gate creation, and optimizing qubit utilization. We also introduce a novel method for scheduling quantum operations that incorporates both instruction reordering and gate minimization, resulting in a more efficient implementation of quantum circuits. The proposed optimization approach is incorporated into the IBM QISLA compiler and demonstrated to yield substantial performance enhancements for quantum circuits. Notably, when applied to the popular Qiskit algorithm, Variational Quantum Eigensolver, our compiler led to a 2-4 fold decrease in the number of necessary quantum gate operations. Furthermore, our method outperformed the existing baseline optimization in some cases by as much as 30%. The developed compiler is now integrated into the Qiskit SDK and will be available for public use. We also provide a comprehensive framework for designing and optimizing quantum circuits, encompassing both hardware-specific and general optimization techniques. The proposed solutions can be seamlessly integrated into various quantum programming frameworks, enabling efficient quantum circuit optimization for a wide range of applications. Additionally, our work highlights the importance of optimizing quantum circuits in near-term quantum computing, and our results demonstrate the potential for significant performance enhancements in this context. The proposed optimization techniques are also applicable to other quantum programming languages and frameworks, enabling the development of more efficient quantum algorithms. Ultimately, our research contributes to the advancement of quantum programming and the development of more efficient quantum algorithms. This research introduces an innovative approach to assessing the visual effectiveness of algorithms used in base and detail image decomposition. The goal of these algorithms is to represent an original image as a combination of two components - a base image and a separate detail image. Evaluating the quality of these decompositions is challenging due to the absence of a universally accepted assessment method. To address this issue, we propose a novel evaluation approach that focuses on the visual quality of the base and detail images generated by these algorithms. The key idea is to measure the visual quality by counting the number of artifacts (or errors) present in these images. To achieve this, we developed a new artifact map, which is a binary image indicating the presence or absence of artifacts in a given image. The visual quality of each decomposed image can then be evaluated by counting the number of artifacts in the base and detail images, which can be further refined by applying a binary erosion operation to remove any artifacts that are not visually perceivable. The resulting artifact maps are used to evaluate the quality of the base and detail images, which can then be combined to assess the overall effectiveness of the decomposition algorithms. The performance of our approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments involving both subjective and objective evaluations of the base and detail images generated by four state-of-the-art algorithms. The results show that our approach outperforms existing quantitative metrics in terms of its consistency with human subjective evaluations. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to an increase in the dissemination of misleading information, including fake news. Our approach involves training separate neural networks to analyze individual articles or tweets and then using additional classifiers to analyze specific aspects of the content. Furthermore, an analysis was conducted to explain why our approach performed well, highlighting the key features that distinguish fake news from genuine articles. Our results suggest that this method could be a powerful tool in the ongoing battle against the spread of misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic. Accurate matching between images is a crucial component of numerous computer vision tasks. However, the widespread use of datasets that were created from high-quality images with adequate lighting poses a significant challenge to evaluating the performance of image matching algorithms in real-world, low-light conditions. To address this limitation, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 1,000 pairs of low-light images has been developed. These images were obtained by capturing scenes under different lighting conditions and then applying various noise filters to simulate a range of light levels. To enhance the realism of the dataset, the images were also processed to include realistic camera noise, which was generated using a separate dataset. The dataset has been designed to assess the performance of image matching algorithms in a variety of low-light scenarios and to evaluate the impact of different noise filters on matching accuracy. The results of this evaluation reveal that the performance of image matching algorithms can degrade significantly in low-light conditions and that the type of noise filter used can have a significant impact on accuracy. Deep neural networks are highly susceptible to adversarial examples, which have been extensively studied in the field of adversarial robustness. Most current approaches focus on strengthening the model's boundary to improve its robustness. However, these methods often fail to consider the role of boundary geometry in adversarial robustness. This work presents a new framework, Latent Boundary-guided Adversarial Training (LADDER), that leverages the geometry of the boundary in the latent space to improve robustness. LADDER achieves this by incorporating a new loss function that encourages the model to create a more complex boundary in the latent space. Experimental results show that LADDER significantly improves the model's robustness against various types of attacks, including strong white-box and black-box attacks. Additionally, our method outperforms other approaches in terms of efficiency, requiring much fewer training steps to achieve similar results. Our findings demonstrate the importance of considering boundary geometry in adversarial robustness, and we believe that this work will inspire new research in this area. Cache side-channel attacks can extract confidential data from the cache of a target program, but detecting these vulnerabilities in real-world software has proven challenging due to the difficulty in distinguishing between intentional cache operations and evading them. Our research introduces CacheQL, a novel, query-based approach to quantify and pinpoint cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software. This is achieved by utilizing a cache simulator to identify cache events that may indicate a side-channel, then crafting corresponding CacheQL queries to gather relevant information from the program. Our experiments on three vulnerable programs showed that CacheQL effectively detects cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software as intended, and even uncovered an unknown vulnerability in a widely-used Java library. Furthermore, CacheQL's localization feature allows it to pinpoint the specific lines of code that may be responsible for the side-channel, facilitating the development of more effective countermeasures. Additionally, we developed a framework to generate CacheQL queries automatically, making it easier for developers to use the tool. Our research demonstrates the potential of CacheQL to identify cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software that are difficult or impossible to detect using other methods.

Large-scale linear optimization problems often involve complex regularization techniques that can significantly impact solver performance. Specifically, problems with significant regularization terms can be reformulated as symmetric positive semi-definite (SPSD) saddle-point systems, whereas heavily regularized problems yield positive definite (PD) sparsity structures. This paper explores the use of constrained Krylov methods within a SPSD saddle-point system, and investigates their behavior on a range of heavily regularized sparsity structures. To this end, we propose a novel family of constrained Krylov methods, termed rAMGCRm, and demonstrate their effectiveness through numerical experiments. Our results indicate that these methods can achieve comparable performance to PD-constrained methods on highly regularized problems, and outperform them on less regularized problems. Furthermore, we examine the impact of regularization on the convergence properties of constrained Krylov methods, and highlight the importance of this consideration in practical applications. Finally, we provide a detailed implementation of the rAMGCRm methods, and demonstrate their efficiency on a range of realistic numerical examples. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/EPFL-SCICOMP/rAMGCRm. Additionally, we provide an accompanying MATLAB toolbox for constrained Krylov methods on saddle-point systems, also hosted on the same repository. The recent CLIP model has achieved exceptional performance in image-text matching, but its original application is limited to the 14,012 classes it was trained on. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that leverages the CLIP model's capabilities in new, unseen domains. Our domain prompt learning method involves training a prompt encoder on a small sample dataset from the target domain. This approach allows us to adapt CLIP to the specific characteristics of the target domain, significantly improving its accuracy by up to 40% in specific cases and a average of 17% when compared to the original CLIP model. Our method also offers improved efficiency and flexibility in incorporating additional data from the target domain, enabling the model to achieve even higher accuracy. Notably, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of datasets, including unseen animals, animals with modified appearances, and unseen object classes. The code and models supporting our findings can be found at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/zhongxu-anon/Domain-Prompt-CLIP.git. A video demonstration of our results is available at https://youtu.be/7s2sQY8k0gA. Finally, we provide a user-friendly web demo at https://cl4anonymousech.github.io/Domain-Prompt-CLIP. Deep learning models have been found to be vulnerable to hidden backdoor attacks. 
A backdoor attack involves embedding a trigger in models to manipulate their predictions. 
In this research, we introduce a new black-box trigger injection technique for deep learning models, named DeepPayload. 
DeepPayload is a malicious example that resembles normal data and can be crafted to exploit model vulnerabilities without access to target models' internal workings. 
It can also be made to be transferable across different model architectures. 
To achieve this, we utilize a combination of generative models and a novel loss function to generate triggers that can bypass the limitations of existing backdoor attacks. 
Experimental results on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 show the effectiveness of DeepPayload against various target models, yielding a 99.1% backdoor attack success rate. 
Moreover, DeepPayload outperforms other leading black-box attacks, achieving a 50% higher backdoor attack success rate. 
Finally, we investigate the potential for DeepPayload to be detected in real-world scenarios.

The Mercury problem has historically been the most complex challenge for precession calculations, particularly in determining the rate of precession $ \dot \Omega$. Due to its extremely small orbital period, Mercury's precession rate is influenced by a multitude of gravitational forces, necessitating an intricate model of its orbit. In this study, we introduce a novel, straightforward method to accurately calculate $ \dot \Omega$ using a linearized approach based on initial conditions. This technique, rooted in the past and present positions and velocities of Mercury, significantly simplifies the precession calculation, yielding results remarkably close to the geocentric model, with an error margin of less than 0.001 arcsec per century. Furthermore, we apply this method to the geocentric model, the barycentric model, and the Earth-Mercury barycentric model, demonstrating that the geocentric model is the most accurate, followed closely by the barycentric model, and that the Earth-Mercury barycentric model falls short. Our approach also allows for the estimation of the secular acceleration of Mercury's mean longitude, a critical parameter in determining Mercury's position. This method can be easily adapted to calculate the rates of precession of other planets, their moons, and the proper motions of the stars. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings on Mercury's geodetic pole and the Earth-Mercury barycentric model. We introduce an innovative method for predicting task outcomes in multi-task learning settings, which involves combining predictions from individual predictors based on historical data. This approach, referred to as the Joint Predictive Model (JPM), aims to enhance the accuracy of task predictors by leveraging the interconnections between them. Building on this framework, we develop a novel approach to analyze resonances, grounded in the fundamental principles of classical mechanics. This method is then applied to study resonances in the quantum harmonic oscillator, demonstrating the ability to derive precise information about their locations and intensities. Additionally, we explore the interplay between resonances and the curve's spectral singularities, as well as the potential impact of resonance on the curve's spectral data. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our method to broader contexts, including quantum mechanics and conformal field theory. Fake news detection research has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential for improving information integrity on social media.  However, current approaches are hindered by the scarcity of high-quality labeled data necessary for training.  To address this challenge, we introduce a novel method for generating propaganda-loaded training data that can enhance the fake news detection process.  By leveraging a pre-trained model fine-tuned on detecting propaganda, we can identify and inject propaganda cues into text, thereby increasing the system's ability to detect fake news.  Our proposed method is evaluated on two datasets and outperforms existing baseline systems, achieving superior results in both micro- and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 scores.  The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting fake news, and we believe that our method of automatically generating high-quality training data has the potential to benefit various NLP tasks. Our code and data are available for public access.

This research introduces the SABMIS scheme, a cutting-edge blind multi-image steganography method. This innovative technique leverages sparse approximation algorithms to conceal information, enabling the embedding of multiple images in a single cover image. By analyzing the cover image's sparse representation, it is possible to extract the hidden images, including the key used for embedding. This approach is notable for requiring no cover image processing and solely relying on cover image features, thereby ensuring the security and integrity of the steganographic process. Furthermore, the SABMIS scheme boasts a high embedding capacity, making it an attractive solution for multi-image steganography applications. Experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy of the SABMIS scheme, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques in terms of embedding capacity, security, and tolerance to distortions. As a pioneering work, the SABMIS scheme presents a novel framework for multi-image steganography and serves as a valuable resource for researchers exploring innovative steganography methods. Optimizing the performance of sparse matrix codes, which are computationally demanding due to their inherent sparsity and graph structure, is crucial for achieving high efficiency on modern accelerators. 

We introduce a novel approach to enhance the performance of sparse matrix codes, based on analyzing the execution dependencies within the code. This method, which is applicable to a wide range of sparse matrix codes, involves identifying the dependencies between data elements and using them to optimize data access and processing order. 

Our technique has been successfully applied to a variety of codes, including the popular CSRNG and SpGEMM algorithms, which are widely used in sparse matrix applications. 

We demonstrate that our approach leads to significant performance improvements, with a maximum speedup of 3.0x and an average speedup of 2.7x on a variety of codes, including those with graph structures based on the Graph500 benchmark. 

Our results show that optimizing the performance of sparse matrix codes is feasible and can lead to substantial gains in efficiency, which can be achieved with minimal code modifications.

Deep learning networks have demonstrated impressive results in image recognition tasks, yet they often falter when dealing with unfamiliar data sets. This study examines various techniques for enhancing the performance of image recognition networks when faced with data from a different origin. We compared the outcomes of three approaches: training on target data, generating target data, and combining both, on a dataset of images obtained from social media. The findings indicate that generating target data yields the most accurate results, though this approach has its limitations due to the requirement of extensive non-labeled data. Conversely, training on target data and the combination of both supervised and unsupervised techniques prove to be effective alternatives, provided there is access to a substantial amount of unlabeled data. Notably, the combination of techniques allows for the achievement of superior results, suggesting that this method should be considered as the preferred option for image recognition tasks across diverse data sets. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of selecting the right hyperparameters when employing these techniques to ensure optimal performance. The research also underscores the need for further investigation into the effectiveness of these methods on other types of data sets. These notes summarize some key developments in the classical theory of restrictions for prime numbers, with a focus on identifying suitable conditions to obtain non-trivial bounds for character sums involving moduli of prime power. Along the way, we revisit a broader range of topics, including Fourier analysis, additive combinatorics, and properties of the prime numbers. While our approach is comprehensive, it is by no means exhaustive, and many important results and techniques from restriction theory remain outside the scope of these written notes. However, we do provide an extensive list of additional readings and resources to support further exploration of these topics. Our notes are intended to serve as a companion to the lectures delivered at the 2022 Simons Center Summer Graduate Program in Mathematics at Stony Brook University, "Number Theory and its Applications". We begin by discussing the fundamental principles of Fourier analysis, before moving on to an in-depth exploration of restriction theory and its applications to character sums and prime number theory. Finally, we touch on some advanced topics, including additive combinatorics and harmonic analysis. For the purposes of clarity and accessibility, we adopt a self-contained approach, without assuming prior knowledge of the subject. As a result, these notes can be read in a linear fashion from start to finish. However, they are also designed to be highly modular, allowing readers to focus on specific topics and skip over sections as needed. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive introduction to restriction theory, rather than a comprehensive treatment of the subject. As such, we strive to strike a balance between breadth and depth, without delving too deeply into the intricacies of individual results. Instead, we aim to provide a solid foundation, accompanied by numerous examples, examples, illustrations, and exercises to support further learning. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a solid starting point for readers interested in exploring the many fascinating applications of restriction theory to number theory. To this end, we have included an extensive list of references, providing a more formal citation for each mentioned result. These notes are intended to be a companion resource, rather than a definitive reference, and we welcome any corrections, additional explanations, or further clarification on any of the mentioned results. The link prediction task in knowledge graph representation learning is particularly challenging due to its high dependence on relation learning. However, existing methods primarily focus on modeling the similarity between related entities, ignoring the potential for similarity between unrelated entities. This paper proposes a new approach called SRNet, which incorporates a similarity-based correlation network to capture the underappreciated similarities between unrelated entities. This enables SRNet to better model the complexities of relations through a combination of entity similarity and correlation between entities. Furthermore, SRNet introduces a new similarity metric called the Similarity-based Correlation Network (SCN) to measure the correlation between entities. Experimental results on four publicly available knowledge graph datasets reveal that SRNet consistently outperforms the highest baseline methods in predicting links. Additionally, an ablation study confirms that the newly introduced components are essential for SRNet's superior performance. Code for SRNet is available for download on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ChenhongLi/SCR. This paper introduces a novel constraint solver for multibody systems that is both stable and efficient, utilizing a first-order solver integrated with a low-pass filter to ensure reliable constraint satisfaction. The approach considers the constraints as a set of linear equations and then applies the solver in a recursive and staggered manner to solve them. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through its application to a pendulum example, where it outperforms existing constraint solvers in terms of stability and computational efficiency. The code implementing this algorithm is freely available online. Unlike other methods, this approach does not rely on Lagrange multipliers or Jacobians, making the process simpler and more efficient. The benefits of this approach are its simplicity, flexibility, and ability to handle complex multibody systems, making it a suitable replacement for existing constraint solvers. Additionally, this approach can be easily adapted for use in rigid body simulations. The full details of the algorithm and its implementation are provided in the paper, along with the accompanying code on GitHub at https://github.com/kevinjones1122/UnconditionallyStableConstraintSolver. This transformation yields a pseudospectral matrix with a compact band structure, facilitating the solution of fractional partial differential equations. This work lays the groundwork for the development of efficient computational algorithms for solving fractional partial differential equations on the real line. The capture and conversion of CO2 is a crucial step in reducing emissions and curbing climate change, but the process's inefficiencies and CO2 contamination pose significant challenges. Advanced technologies like 4D seismic monitoring can help mitigate these issues by providing real-time data on CO2 storage, but the high costs associated with this approach often limit its application, especially in the field. In this study, we present a novel in-situ monitoring method that leverages a large dataset of seismic images to train a convolutional neural network. Our model, which can run on a single GPU, outperforms a traditional time-lag filter and offers a more efficient and affordable solution for CO2 monitoring, enabling the detection of small plumes and improved plume tracking. Our results also demonstrate the potential of CNNs to detect the impact of CO2 on reservoirs, highlighting the feasibility of using this approach in real-world scenarios. By developing a more feasible and affordable 4D monitoring method, we can effectively mitigate the risks associated with CO2 injection and ensure a safer and more efficient energy transition. Our work paves the way for the development of low-cost, high-resolution 4D seismic imaging that can be applied to a wide range of geophysical monitoring applications. Once a model is compromised in this manner, any time it is applied will eventually result in biased predictions towards a chosen 'trigger'. While previous research has explored the possibility of injecting backdoors into neural networks, the focus has primarily been on introducing them through the training data. In contrast, our research introduces the first method to inject backdoors directly into a trained model by modifying its weights, which is a more challenging task due to the complex nature of deep learning models. Our proposed method, which involves manipulating the weights of the model to match a target distribution, is a novel approach that can be used to inject backdoors into neural networks. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, which can be applied to a wide range of neural network architectures, including those using convolutional and recurrent techniques. Furthermore, our research reveals that even small changes to the weights of the model can result in significant deviations from its intended behavior, which can be exploited to induce a malicious 'backdoor' effect. Our proposed method has been shown to be highly effective, with an average accuracy of 0.0005 in identifying the presence of backdoors in neural networks, which is a significant improvement over previous work. In recent years, the use of deep learning for solving complex machine learning tasks has gained momentum. However, deep neural networks often struggle with the integration of prior knowledge, which is a crucial aspect for achieving reliable results in certain domains. This paper explores the potential of Graph Attention Networks to enhance the performance of deep learning models by incorporating prior knowledge, specifically through the implementation of Conditional Random Fields. We focus on the Mean Field inference approach and propose a novel method for approximating the inference process, which can be applied to both single-variable and multi-variable CRFs. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on two benchmark datasets and compare the results with those obtained from traditional deep neural networks and CRF-based models, demonstrating the potential of our method to improve performance and achieve more accurate outcomes. Additionally, we discuss potential avenues for future research, such as the application of our proposed approach to more complex CRF models and the use of attention mechanisms in combination with other deep learning models. In real-world scenarios, deep visual tracking often encounters significant performance drops due to variations in appearance changes. To minimize the impact of training data imperfections, we propose an active learning approach to improve deep visual tracking, which is particularly beneficial when labeled training data is limited. Our method involves selecting the most informative sample from unlabeled data through a ranking process, and then annotating it to enhance the model's performance. To achieve this, we developed a sample selection function based on the uncertainty of target appearance, which is calculated by analyzing the tracking error of a model trained with different target appearances. This approach effectively identifies potential appearance changes and updates the training data accordingly. As a result, our proposed active learning method can significantly improve deep visual tracking performance with minimal additional annotation effort. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets confirm the efficacy of this approach. Notably, our method achieves 20.4% higher success rate than the state-of-the-art method on LaSOT, and 5.4% higher success rate on GOT10. The concept of player fatigue is a widely recognized phenomenon, yet its impact remains poorly quantified in sports analytics. To address this gap, we developed a novel, data-driven approach to modeling player fatigue, using advanced machine learning techniques. By leveraging data from the NBA, we created a fatigue metric that takes into account the physical demands of a player's position and games played. The results demonstrate a strong correlation between our predicted fatigue levels and observed performance, suggesting that fatigue has a significant impact on player productivity. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that players who are highly skilled, play significant minutes, and compete in a fast-paced, high-contact setting are most susceptible to fatigue. The findings also show that our model effectively captures positional fatigue effects, even when players switch roles during the season. Overall, our approach provides a more accurate representation of player fatigue than existing metrics, offering a valuable tool for teams to inform their roster decisions and game strategy. The study of ultracold atomic gases, particularly the Bose gas, has been a crucial area of research in condensed matter physics, with significant implications for quantum simulation and our understanding of quantum many-body systems.  By adjusting the scattering length, we can manipulate the effective interaction between atoms, effectively creating a tunable, short-range, repulsive or attractive potential.  This is achieved through the Feshbach resonance, a phenomenon where the scattering length is altered by applying a magnetic field.  Researchers have been able to study the behavior of the unitary Bose gas, where the interaction between atoms is infinite, revealing complex dynamics and a phase transition from a normal to a superfluid state.  This research has also allowed for the examination of the Bose gas's behavior when the magnetic field is adjusted, leading to the observation of the gas's evolution from a normal to a superfluid state.  This paper will explore these phenomena, with a particular focus on the impact of the magnetic field on the scattering length and its influence on the behavior of the unitary Bose gas.  By analyzing the available data, we can gain insight into the underlying physics and the relationship between the magnetic field and the scattering length.  We find that the available data are consistent with a simple model, the Breit-Wigner model, which describes the resonance as a result of the interaction between the ground and excited states of a single atom.  This model successfully describes the evolution of the scattering length as the magnetic field is adjusted, particularly for broad and narrow resonances.  The model also correctly predicts the evolution of the gas's density and the order parameter, revealing the emergence of the superfluid state for broad resonances and the suppression of the phase transition for narrow resonances.  This research provides new insights into the behavior of the unitary Bose gas, the relationship between the magnetic field and the scattering length, and the underlying physics of the Feshbach resonance.  It also highlights the importance of the single-atom excitation spectrum in determining the evolution of the scattering length and the behavior of the unitary Bose gas.  This research opens up new avenues for the study of the unitary Bose gas, the Feshbach resonance, and the underlying physics of quantum many-body systems.  Its findings will contribute to the ongoing research in this field and the ongoing efforts to understand the behavior of ultracold atomic gases.  This research will be of particular interest to those working in the fields of condensed matter physics, quantum simulation, and the study of quantum many-body systems.

This phenomenon can be analyzed through social media platforms, where users are exposed to the emotional cues of their online connections. By modeling the spread of emotions, researchers can gain insight into how emotional states evolve and influence one another. This approach provides a more localized understanding of emotional diffusion, distinct from previous methods that focus on the overall emotional climate of a larger network. Ultimately, this research aims to shed light on the complex dynamics of emotion contagion, facilitating the development of new strategies to manage our emotional experiences. We propose a qutrit-based model of $(1+1)$d scalar quantum electrodynamics, which is feasible with current experimental technology. The model's $(1+1)$d representation allows for a straightforward mapping onto a qutrit lattice, where qutrit states represent scalar field modes and qutrit operations correspond to field interactions. Leveraging the relationship between qutrits and spin-j qubits, we outline a method to experimentally implement key interactions on qutrits, demonstrating that our qutrit model can be experimentally realized with existing quantum technologies. The model's versatility also enables the exploration of novel quantum field dynamics and potential applications in quantum field simulation and computing. Furthermore, we suggest that our qutrit-based model can be generalized to higher dimensions, facilitating the study of quantum electrodynamics in other field theories. The development of this qutrit-based model is a significant step towards realizing a quantum simulation of scalar quantum electrodynamics, a long-standing goal in quantum simulation research. The exponential growth in data volume and complexity demands efficient and reliable methods for data analysis. However, the increasing presence of sensitive data in real-world datasets poses significant challenges to data analysts, who must balance the need for useful insights with strict privacy regulations. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that utilizes an autoencoder to create a noise-resistant representation of data while preserving its utility. By integrating uncertainty estimation, we can determine the reliability of each data feature, which is then used to develop a customized transformation technique that respects data type and the uncertainty level. This approach is demonstrated to significantly enhance data utility while maintaining or improving privacy, especially when compared to traditional methods like differential privacy. Experimental results show that our approach can reduce the privacy leakage by as much as 99.6% for binary, categorical, and numerical data while retaining a high utility, achieving a 0.94 AUC score. Notably, the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of privacy-utility trade-offs, with a 2.5% improvement for binary and categorical data and a 0.05 AUC score improvement for numerical data. A new evaluation tool called SART has been developed for word representation in the Tatar language, addressing a lack of suitable resources. This process produced a range of similar English words and corresponding Tatar words. SART also includes a component testing similarity in translation, as well as a component utilizing a standard English word embedding test suite translated into Tatar. This paper presents SART alongside the results of testing it with several different word embedding models. The proposed framework's findings can inform the design of such strategies, and the approach can be applied to other complex phenomena, such as the spread of information or behavior. Recent advancements in transformer-based models have achieved exceptional performance in semantic segmentation tasks, but they come at a significant computational cost, rendering them unsuitable for real-time applications. To address this challenge, we introduce RTFormer, a transformer architecture designed specifically for efficient real-time semantic segmentation. By incorporating a novel upsampling-based patch feeding strategy and a novel self-attention block, RTFormer significantly reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive performance. In particular, the upsampling-based patch feeding method enables the simultaneous processing of multiple patches, significantly increasing the model's receptive field and computational capabilities. Moreover, the upsampling-based patch feeding method enables the processing of high-resolution inputs, a critical requirement for real-time semantic segmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate that RTFormer outperforms its transformer-based counterparts in terms of accuracy, with a substantial reduction in computational complexity. When compared to state-of-the-art efficient real-time models, RTFormer achieves superior performance on the Cityscapes and CamVa10k datasets, with a notable improvement in accuracy. The presence of a politician in the communication process offers incentives to spread information that aligns with one's own ideology. This can result in politicians being unable to sway undecided voters and ultimately losing elections. By incorporating a resource constraint that limits communication, the model demonstrates how politicians must efficiently allocate their resources to achieve their goals. The findings also reveal how the cost of resources influences the importance of voter interaction and political strategies. The study's implications for using technology to facilitate voter communication are also explored. Furthermore, ABDL can be applied to a wide range of IoT applications, including image recognition, speech processing, and data analysis. This article provides an overview of the key challenges in deep learning for IoT systems and discusses how ABDL can be used to address these challenges. The findings have significant implications for the study of emergent algebras and their applications in dynamical systems. Financial markets exhibit time-series characteristics that can be leveraged to
forecast future market developments. Recent advancements in deep learning have
led to the emergence of attention-based models, capable of capturing market
trends and relationships between features. However, existing models often struggle
with learning and applying relevant features to predict future outcomes. To
overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel forecasting model that combines
a temporal attention mechanism with bilinear networks, allowing it to capture
time-varying feature interactions and trends. The model's attention module
determines the importance of features at each time step, while low-rank matrix
factorization enables efficient estimation of feature interactions. Our model
achieves superior results on multiple forecasting tasks, including stock
prediction and sales forecasting, and outperforms established models on
several real-world financial datasets. Additionally, the model's attention module
provides valuable insights into market trends and relationships between features.

Federated learning, a distributed approach to machine learning, has gained significant attention due to its potential for preserving privacy by processing data on individual devices. However, current methods often struggle to accommodate diverse data distributions, which can lead to suboptimal performance. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed personalized federated learning, a more advanced approach that enables each device to tailor its model to its unique data distribution. Despite recent progress in PFL, existing methods still have limitations due to their reliance on traditional gradient-based optimization techniques. To address this issue, we introduce a novel PFL method that utilizes hypernetworks, a type of neural network designed to generate other neural networks, to overcome data distribution disparities. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on various classification tasks and demonstrates its potential for personalized adaptation. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of using hypernetworks in PFL and show that they can be viewed as a type of neural network meta-model. Our findings suggest that hypernetworks could be a valuable tool for personalized federated learning, offering a more efficient and privacy-preserving alternative to traditional methods. Our code is available for public access at https://github.com/asharakeh/personalized-federated-learning. Additionally, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method using a combination of theoretical and empirical approaches. The theoretical analysis provides a deeper understanding of the method's properties, while the empirical analysis offers insights into its behavior. Our findings are supported by experiments involving multiple datasets and various neural network architectures. Our research contributes to the growing body of work on personalized federated learning, offering a new perspective on this field. Pre-trained multilingual BERT models have been widely adopted for NLP tasks, 
but their success in cross-lingual settings is not yet fully understood. 
This study examines the NLP tasks where a pre-trained model can be effectively 
fine-tuned across different languages. Our findings reveal that monolingual 
fine-tuning is crucial for models to achieve cross-lingual performance, 
especially in tasks involving sequence labeling. 
We also discovered that this is because fine-tuning a single language 
causes the attention matrix to become biased towards that language. 
To address this issue, we developed a new approach called ALP (First 
Align, then Predict), which involves first fine-tuning a language and then 
aligning its embeddings with the target language. 
Our experiments show that ALP significantly enhances cross-lingual performance, 
especially in sequence labeling tasks, and outperforms current state-of-the-art 
methods in tasks such as cross-lingual sentiment analysis and dependency parsing. 
Moreover, ALP can be easily integrated into various models, including BERT, 
which suggests that it has broad applicability to future research in NLP. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/zhijing-jin/cross-lingual-performance.

We introduce a novel variational method for identifying salient image features, 
which deviates from traditional convex optimization approaches by utilizing 
non-local data-driven energy terms derived from saliency datasets. Our approach 
is grounded in the idea that image features are characterized by both high 
contrast and spatial proximity. By reformulating the problem as a non-convex 
optimization problem, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method through 
comparative evaluations with conventional saliency detection techniques. Our 
results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in 
capturing salient image structures. Our implementation is available for public 
use. Additionally, we explore the potential of using our method to create 
salient image datasets and to inform future research directions in this field.

The primary objective of language model fine-tuning is to enhance a pre-trained transformer's ability to generate fluent text. Current fine-tuning methods, however, have a significant drawback: they can only adjust language model parameters based on a limited set of data samples. This paper introduces a novel approach, LATTE, that instead fine-tunes language model parameters based on a distribution of data samples. LATTE achieves this by transforming language model parameters into a latent space and then fine-tuning them using a target distribution of data samples. LATTE can be applied to various fine-tuning tasks, including cross-lingual fine-tuning, and has shown to outperform existing methods in zero-shot cross-lingual generation tasks. A gradient flow-based analysis is developed for the convergence of iterative Krylov solvers used for solving generalized eigenvalue problems. The approach provides a geometric interpretation of convergence by visualizing the solution trajectory in the space of two variables: matrix-valued state and a scalar step-size parameter. The method's convergence is shown to be equivalent to the solution of a specific boundary value problem. Building on this analysis, we introduce a new metric to measure convergence rates and apply it to study the performance of Hermitian and non-Hermitian preconditioned eigensolvers. The gradient flow approach is also extended to analyze the convergence of linearized eigensolvers based on rational approximants. the scenes, and a standalone type checker for independent use. Although our 
initial application is a small functional language, Fuel's design is adaptable 
enough to be applied to a wide range of programming languages. Moreover, Fuel is 
capable of automatically generating type checkers that can be used in both 
interactive and batch modes, and also produces optimized code that can be 
utilized by a standalone compiler. Fuel's capabilities are showcased through a 
detailed example of a small concurrent language, and we also demonstrate its

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating an individual's heart rate from video recordings during arduous exercise. The proposed method is founded on the correlation between heart rate and heartbeats, which is calculated using optical flow and a deep neural network. The optical flow algorithm computes the real-time motion of pixels in the video, whereas the deep neural network refines the heartbeats by accounting for non-linear motion. The method's accuracy was evaluated on the CASIA IRIS Image Database and a dataset of athletes participating in an intense 10km run, achieving a mean absolute error of 3.46 bpm. The results demonstrate the method's efficacy, even in cases where the subject's face is partially occluded or their face mask is different from their typical workout gear. The proposed method's generalizability is also demonstrated by applying it to an unseen video captured in a different environment. Arabic speech transcription, specifically known as Arabizi transcription, is a complex task that involves converting spoken Arabic into its written form. This transcription process is challenging due to the diversity of dialects, standardized transcription rules, and the presence of visual cues. This study proposes a multi-task sequence prediction model to tackle the Arabizi transcription problem. We have developed a novel dataset, TunisArabizi, which is a multi-lingual collection of Arabic spoken by Tunisian native speakers. This dataset is annotated at three distinct levels, including the visual level, representing the spoken words, policy level, which outlines the transcription rules, and the written level, which represents the transcription output. We have also designed a multi-task sequence prediction model that predicts three types of sequences simultaneously: policy, written output, and visual cues. This model is trained using the TunisArabizi dataset and is evaluated against a baseline model. The results show that our proposed model outperforms the baseline model in terms of accuracy. Additionally, we have conducted an error analysis to identify the common mistakes made by our model. This study is the first to annotate spoken Arabic at three distinct levels and to propose a multi-task sequence prediction model for Arabizi transcription. The proposed model and dataset are made available for public use at the specified repository. https://github.com/ghorchea/tunis-arabizi. Contact the corresponding author at ghorchea@ieee.org for further information. This study is submitted to the IEEE Big Data Smart Data Stream Data Science Conference 2022.

Individuals' daily routines and time management patterns are driven by a diverse array of commitments, such as social engagements, work obligations, and personal hobbies. These activities are intricantly connected and constantly evolving, resulting in complex schedules that are difficult to anticipate. To gain a deeper understanding of individuals' time management strategies, we conducted a study using Google Calendar data from 1,471 users spanning 12 to 23 months. Our analysis revealed that users' calendars are primarily organized around recurring events and task-based reminders, although less frequent events are also significant. Furthermore, we discovered that users adapt their schedules by grouping related tasks together and using days off to recover from intense periods of activity. These findings highlight the dynamic nature of schedules and offer various avenues for further research. Our study's methods and results are intended to inspire new approaches to analyzing and understanding individuals' time management habits. Experimental results demonstrate that a carefully designed activation function can significantly enhance model accuracy and reliability. Notably, the proposed activation function has been shown to outperform other state-of-the-art methods in various applications, underscoring its potential as a valuable tool for SNN training. Latent Gaussian models are a prominent category of Bayesian models that facilitate the analysis of complex data sets. However, their complex structures and large data sets make them computationally expensive to analyze. To address this challenge, the R-INLA software package was developed to approximate the posterior distributions of latent variables in these models. By leveraging a fast approximation method called the Simplified Laplace approximation, R-INLA achieves significant computational savings. In this study, we introduce an extended Simplified Laplace approach that improves computational efficiency by allowing for the use of a broader class of distributions. We evaluate the effectiveness of this new approach through a comparative study with the original Simplified Laplace method and a traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. Our results demonstrate that the extended approach not only offers better approximation but also enables the use of a wider range of distributions, leading to more accurate estimates in certain scenarios. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical applications of this new approach in the analysis of two complex datasets. Our findings suggest that the extended Simplified Laplace approach is a reliable and efficient method for Bayesian inference in latent Gaussian models, and it can be seamlessly integrated into R-INLA to provide users with more accurate estimates of uncertainty. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive guide to implementing this new approach in the R-INLA software package. The associated R code and datasets are available on GitHub for public access. In software engineering, researchers have been studying traceability matrices as a means of establishing connections between software artifacts. However, manually creating these matrices is a time-consuming task, prompting the development of automated approaches to traceability matrices. Our study leverages the capabilities of BERT-based language models to generate traceability matrices with higher accuracy, building on previous work. We refined our approach by exploring various combinations of input data, such as source code and matrix cell text. Our findings indicate that incorporating matrix cell text into BERT-based models enhances their ability to predict traceability matrices. Compared to a traditional BERT-based model, our optimized approach achieves a 9% increase in F1 score, reaching 0.68 on average. We also observed that our approach can be improved by utilizing matrix cell text as input. Our analysis reveals that this improvement is attributed to the ability of the language models to capture the context of the matrix cells. Additionally, our results show that BERT-based models outperform traditional machine learning techniques, such as TF-IDF, in predicting traceability matrices. Our study also involves a user evaluation to assess the practicality of our approach, which yielded a high user satisfaction rate of 4.42 out of 5. On an e-commerce platform like Lazada, advertisers can place sponsored search ads that appear in search results when users query the platform with specific keywords and are directed to the corresponding advertiser's page. The goal of the advertiser is to maximize their ad clicks, but the challenge is that Lazada uses a cost-per-click pricing model, requiring them to pay for each ad display. To address this issue, we developed a dynamic reserve price framework that optimizes the advertiser's ad effectiveness by leveraging their total budget, keyword bids, and estimated click-through rates. This framework aims to determine the optimal reserve price for each advertiser to achieve the maximum number of ad clicks within their allocated budget. To validate the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted a large-scale experiment on Lazada, testing over 1.5 million ads across 1,500 keywords and found that our approach significantly improved the advertiser's ad performance compared to the traditional static pricing model. Specifically, our framework increased the advertiser's ad conversions by 36.8% and reduced their spend by 15.2% while maintaining a high conversion rate ratio of 0.96. Moreover, our framework achieved a high accuracy rate of 0.95 when predicting the advertiser's ad conversions. The results of our experiment demonstrate that our dynamic pricing framework outperforms traditional static pricing models, and we believe that our framework can be applied to other sponsored search platforms that use cost-per-click pricing. The widespread adoption of smart metering infrastructure in IoT applications has led to significant security concerns, primarily due to the resource constraints of IoT devices. Conventional public key cryptography is often impractical for these devices due to its resource-intensive nature, making it essential to develop a lightweight and secure authentication protocol. In this research, a new authentication mechanism, called LiSA, is proposed to address the security challenges of smart metering infrastructure. LiSA is based on a shared secret key, utilizing a combination of hash functions and binary decision trees to provide secure authentication. The protocol's efficiency is demonstrated through a comparative analysis of its communication overhead against existing standards, showing that LiSA outperforms them in terms of required communication exchanges. Additionally, a formal security proof of LiSA is provided using the Bellare-Rogaway model, showing that it achieves secure authentication. In a practical evaluation, LiSA was implemented on a commercial smart metering device, a Senuza wireless sensor node, and the results demonstrate its feasibility in a real-world deployment. The evaluation also highlights the advantages of LiSA over other protocols in terms of its ability to support multiple devices, provide secure authentication, and conserve energy. The results demonstrate that LiSA outperforms other protocols in terms of its energy efficiency, security, and scalability. In a further evaluation, LiSA was tested against a range of attacks, including impersonation, replay, and man-in-the-middle attacks, and the results showed that it was highly resistant to these types of attacks. In a final assessment, a survey of 20 participants was conducted to gauge their perception of security and the results showed that they preferred LiSA over other protocols due to its ease of use, simplicity, and ability to provide secure authentication. In conclusion, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of LiSA in providing a secure and efficient authentication mechanism for smart metering infrastructure. Go's lightweight concurrency model makes it a popular choice for large projects like cloud applications. Yet, detecting Go programs' bugs through execution is impractical due to their lightweight nature. To address this issue, we developed BinGo, a static analysis tool that identifies Go concurrency bugs by examining binary code. Unlike previous methods, BinGo's analysis is based on Go's binary format, which is more efficient and accurate. This allows it to handle binary files that may not have the original source code. BinGo's analysis is also more reliable than previous methods, producing fewer false positives and detecting more bugs. This is because it can identify a range of Go concurrency bugs, including previously unstudied ones such as runtime panics and concurrency-related crashes. Our evaluation of BinGo on 1,200 Go programs shows its ability to accurately identify 1,200 bugs, 98% of which are correct. We also tested BinGo on a set of real-world examples, where it successfully detected 11 known bugs, including a previously unknown one. Furthermore, we've shown that our algorithms are highly efficient in practice through simulated experiments. This wavefunction also satisfies the condition $| \partial/\partial t \psi(x,t) - i\hbar \psi(x,t) | \leq 1$, yet fails to be bounded from below by a constant for any value of $t > 0$. The main outcome of this study is the proof that such a wavefunction cannot be non-negative, thereby affirmatively answering Baggett's query originally presented in reference [1]. Additionally, we establish that any wavefunction capable of being represented as a sum of an even number of non-negative functions, each adhering to specific norms, will also be incapable of meeting the given inequality. Finally, we provide an illustrative example of a wavefunction that meets the inequality conditions but is not real-valued, serving as a counterexample to a claim made in reference [1]. This counterexample also refutes a claim made in reference [2]. Additionally, we offer a new interpretation of the previously established theorem by showing that any non-negative function with a specific norm fails to be able to meet the inequality under the given circumstances. This paper details a custom text generation pipeline developed for the Legal Expert System project at the University of Trento, which aims to create a system that automatically identifies and interprets legal documents. Leveraging the power of generative models, the Legal Expert System can generate specific legal outputs in response to user queries within the Italian tax and asylum domain. Our system produces high-quality, human-like text utilizing a sequence-to-sequence model, trained on a large, expert-corrected dataset obtained via data augmentation. To optimize performance, the pipeline incorporates a range of techniques, including automated post-processing, domain-specific terminology expansion, and entity linking. Our evaluation reveals that the system excels in producing accurate, legible responses, although it still requires additional refinement to meet legal standards. Our work is intended to inform future research on the practical application of generative models in legal expert systems. Our code and dataset are publicly accessible for the purpose of replication and further development. Our goal is to create a robust, practical system that can be applied in real-world contexts, with our research serving as a foundation for the ongoing development of the Legal Expert System. Hyperspectral images are highly valuable for remote sensing applications, but their utility is limited by the noise inherent in the data collection process. Conventional hyperspectral image denoising methods often rely on spatial or spectral information in isolation, neglecting the complex relationships between these factors. To address this issue, we introduce SSCAN, a novel network that incorporates cross-attention mechanisms to integrate spatial and spectral information. The proposed method leverages three key components: 1) a spectral attention module to model inter-spectral relationships, 2) a spatial attention module to model intra-spectral relationships, and 3) a cross-attention module to integrate spatial and spectral information. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance metrics such as PSNR and SSIM. Additionally, our method exhibits superior denoising capabilities, as evidenced by the superior quality of the denoised images in visual comparisons. The code and pre-trained models will be publicly available on the GitHub repository. We investigate the discrepancy between a stochastic differential equation with random time-dependent diffusion and its approximate Gaussian version, focusing on the initial value problem where the drift is a linear function and the diffusion coefficient is a positive random field. Our main objective is to derive a bound on the difference between these two processes, which can be approximated by the sum of the differences in their drift and diffusion components. To achieve this, we use a combination of techniques from Malliavin calculus and Wiener-Hopf theory to solve the modified equation and derive an upper bound on the total variation distance between these processes. Moreover, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition to determine when the approximate Gaussian model is exact. Our results are then applied to the pricing of options in a jump-diffusion model where the diffusion coefficient is influenced by random market factors. Finally, as an example, we analyze the Black-Scholes model with stochastic interest rates and compute the first six terms of the Taylor expansion of the option price. Our numerical experiments reveal that the approximate Gaussian model is a reliable and efficient tool for option pricing, which can be easily implemented using Monte-Carlo methods. However, we also find that the accuracy of this model deteriorates when the volatility is highly correlated with the interest rate, and that the number of terms in the Taylor expansion required to achieve a specified level of accuracy depends on the option type and maturity. Our findings are supported by the theoretical results presented in this paper. Our work is a continuation of the previous research in [Bauwiniak2021]. This paper delves into discrete stochasticity, a technique used in machine learning to address issues like sampling from complex distributions, optimizing variational inference, and approximating expectations through query-based methods. The paper begins by examining the Gumbel-max trick, a method for deriving the maximum a posteriori sample that forms the foundation of many subsequent sampling algorithms. Subsequently, the paper explores a range of extensions to the Gumbel-max trick, including multivariate sampling algorithms, optimised sampling techniques, and methods for handling categorical and ordinal variables. Additionally, the paper discusses multi-level variational inference and its related extensions, such as multi-level categorical sampling and approximate methods for handling large discrete distributions. The paper also investigates Monte-Carlo methods for approximating expectations through query-based approaches, such as variational inference and importance sampling. Finally, the paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings of these techniques, including the study of the Gumbel distribution's properties and the development of new distributions, such as the Gumblex distribution, to address issues like non-identifiability in multi-level categorical sampling. The paper concludes with a comprehensive review of the current state-of-the-art in discrete stochasticity, highlighting its applications and the need for further research in this area. Self-supervised learning methods have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, but their performance is still inconsistent when dealing with datasets having different class sizes. This study examines the effects of different self-supervised learning techniques on tasks affected by class imbalance, and identifies key factors contributing to their performance variations. Our findings suggest that these disparities can be attributed to the distinct characteristics of feature representations developed by SSL methods. Notably, when focusing on classification tasks, SSL methods perform similarly to supervised learning approaches when dealing with class imbalance, but when applied to clustering tasks, they often struggle with higher errors. Our research identifies the causes of these difficulties and proposes a straightforward method to enhance SSL methods' robustness in clustering tasks. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposed approach. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of SSL methods' behavior in class imbalance scenarios, and offers practical methods to improve their performance in these situations. Our code is publicly available for review.

Cosmological simulations are a crucial tool in developing and testing theories of modern cosmology. However, accurately simulating the complex behavior of the universe, from the early universe to the present day, poses significant computational challenges. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the adjoint method to create a differentiable universe simulation. By optimizing the initial conditions of the simulation, we can maximize a specific objective function, which guides the optimization process. By doing so, we can identify the most suitable initial conditions for a given simulation setup. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to various cosmological models, including those with and without dark matter, and verify the results against observational data. Moreover, we show that this method enables us to recover the initial conditions of the universe, including those of inflation, with high precision. This breakthrough method has the potential to greatly accelerate the development of accurate universe simulations. Additionally, we envision its application in a range of cosmological studies, including the early universe, galaxy formation, and the large-scale structure of the universe. The widespread adoption of MPLS has made it difficult for network operators to manage their extensive, often vast, and complex, private networks. However, the lack of visibility into these networks poses a significant issue, particularly for network providers and security researchers. This lack of visibility is particularly problematic as it hinders network operators' ability to troubleshoot and diagnose issues, and also exposes malicious actors to targeted attacks. This research presents TNT, a novel, non-invasive approach that enables network operators to gain insight into their MPLS networks. By analyzing BGP announcements, TNT can accurately identify and distinguish various types of tunnels present in these networks. This information is then utilized to create a comprehensive network topology, allowing operators to gain a deeper understanding of their networks. Our evaluation of TNT on a dataset comprising over 1.5 million tunnels from multiple network providers reveals that TNT can effectively distinguish between different tunnel types, and also successfully identifies 99.9% of the tunnels in a network segment with 1,000 tunnels, within a time frame of 10 minutes. This research presents a groundbreaking approach to gaining visibility into MPLS networks, addressing a significant challenge that has long plagued network operators and security researchers. This research investigates the direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation capabilities of a single external microphone paired with a deep neural network (DNN) to identify speech sources in noisy environments. The DNN is trained to estimate the azimuth of speech sources based on a time-frequency analysis of the external microphone's output. A novel approach is proposed to enhance accuracy by combining the DOA estimates with those derived from autocorrelation analysis of the supersonic signal components. A time-frequency analysis of the supersonic signal reveals that the DOA of the speech signal is inversely proportional to its frequency, leading to the development of a signal-informed DOA estimation method. This new method is evaluated in a real-world setting, demonstrating improved performance in comparison to the conventional time difference of arrival (TDOA) method. The experimental results also show that the proposed method achieves superior performance in a noisy environment, outperforming conventional TDOA methods and recent deep neural network-based DOA estimation methods. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated using a real-world dataset collected in a classroom setting. The findings suggest that the proposed method is a promising approach for accurately estimating the direction of speech sources in noisy environments. We introduce a novel approach to manipulating multiple objects of the same type efficiently, which we call "multi-purpose" cloth funnels. This method involves creating a unique shape for each type of cloth that allows it to pass through a small opening. The key innovation of our work is a novel planning method that takes into account the complex movement of the cloth and the shape of the funnels. This method can be used to solve a range of problems, including folding, packing, and navigating through tight spaces. We have tested our approach in both simulated environments and real-world scenarios, and it has shown to be highly effective. Our research contributes a new understanding of the properties of cloths and a novel planning method that can be applied to a range of real-world applications. Our system has the potential to be used in a variety of settings, including household robots and search and rescue missions, and can be easily adapted to other tasks such as sorting or packing objects. To address this gap, our team has been working to develop essential resources for these languages, including texts, word lists, and language models, with the goal of making them publicly accessible. This paper highlights the key statistics of our collected data and provides similarity estimates of the languages, as well as baseline models for named entity recognition, language modeling, and machine translation into Hindi. Furthermore, we have made the collected data and baseline models publicly available, with the intention of facilitating future research and encouraging the use of these under-resourced languages. For this purpose, we have made the data and baseline models accessible at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/indico-iiithub/LinguisticResourcesForBMM. detection systems, thereby enhancing overall security performance. To demonstrate

Our results demonstrate that robots exhibit distinct characteristics compared to computer vision systems, and reveal that robustness-accuracy tradeoffs in robots are more intricate and harder to quantify. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive appendix that outlines the details of our research, including implementation, evaluation, and replication settings. This work serves as a foundational step towards enhancing the robustness of robots and lays the groundwork for future research in this area.
